title: Photosynthesis & Light
objectives: Measure the rate of photosynthesis by counting oxygen bubbles
Use the inverse square law to explain how light intensity changes with distance
Identify a limiting factor and connect photosynthesis to the carbon cycle (APES 1.5, 9.4)

steps.title: Briefing

npcLines: Every bubble rising from this Elodea plant is oxygen made by photosynthesis. More bubbles per minute means faster photosynthesis.
Use the bench on the right. Keep the bicarbonate at 1% and the water at 25 °C, and change only the lamp distance. That's a fair test.
how: Follow the yellow arrow and the compass at the top of the screen.
Walk with W A S D or the arrow keys. On an iPad, drag the joystick in the bottom-left corner.
When you are close, a button appears at the bottom of the screen. Press E or tap the button.
Read each line, then press Continue.

intro: Plants use light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar, and they release oxygen: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
Elodea lives underwater, so you can see its oxygen as bubbles. Counting bubbles per minute measures how fast photosynthesis is happening.
vocab: How plants make sugar from CO₂ and water using light energy.
How fast something happens, here in bubbles per minute.
The resource in shortest supply, which holds back the rate.

steps.title: Vary the light

sequence.instruction: Run a 1-minute trial with the lamp at 10 cm (1% bicarbonate, 25 °C).
how: Walk to the photosynthesis station (the right bench) and step onto its glowing ring. The experiment panel opens.
On an iPad or phone the panel slides up from the bottom. Close it with ✕ when you are done.
Check that Sodium bicarbonate is 1% and Water temperature is 25 °C.
Press '▶ Run 1-minute trial'. Your count appears in 'Your trials'.

sequence.instruction: Run a trial with the lamp at 20 cm.
how: Move the 'Lamp distance' slider to 20 cm. Leave the other settings alone.

sequence.instruction: Run a trial with the lamp at 30 cm.
Run a trial with the lamp at 40 cm.

feedback.correct: 40 cm trial recorded. You now have a data set.

steps.intro: You will change only the lamp distance and count the bubbles. The bicarbonate (CO₂ source) and water temperature stay the same so the test is fair.
vocab: What you measure: bubbles per minute.
What you keep the same: bicarbonate 1% and 25 °C.

steps.title: Analyze

question.prompt: How many bubbles per minute did you count with the lamp at 20 cm?
help: Find the row in 'Your trials' with Lamp 20 cm and Bicarbonate 1%.
Type the number from its Bubbles/min column.

feedback.incorrect: Check the 20 cm row of your trials table.

question.prompt: Light intensity follows the inverse square law. At 20 cm, what fraction of the 10 cm light intensity reaches the plant? (Give a decimal.)
help: Light spreads out as it travels, so its intensity drops with the square of the distance.
Divide the starting distance by the new distance: 10 ÷ 20.
Square that answer (multiply it by itself).
Write your answer as a decimal.
question.example: From 10 cm to 30 cm: 10 ÷ 30 = 0.333, and 0.333 × 0.333 = 0.11. Only about 11% as much light reaches the plant.

sequence.hint: Doubling the distance gives (1/2)² of the light.

sequence.instruction: Now run a trial at 10 cm with 0% bicarbonate (no added CO₂).

feedback.correct: Trial recorded. Compare it with your 10 cm, 1% trial.

how: Set 'Lamp distance' to 10 cm and Water temperature to 25 °C.
Press '▶ Run 1-minute trial', then compare it with your 10 cm, 1% trial.

question.prompt: With the lamp at 10 cm but no added bicarbonate, the rate dropped sharply. What was limiting photosynthesis?

feedback.correct: Right: plenty of light, but not enough CO₂ to build sugar.
feedback.incorrect: Light was at its strongest. What did you remove?

question.prompt: Ocean phytoplankton and forests do the same photosynthesis as Elodea. Explain how they act as carbon sinks, and describe one human activity that weakens them.
help: Explain what a carbon sink is.
Connect it to photosynthesis: forests and phytoplankton remove CO₂ to build sugar, just like Elodea.
Name one human activity that weakens these sinks (for example deforestation, ocean warming or pollution) and explain how it does that.

steps.intro: Look for a pattern in your data. As the lamp moves farther away, what happens to the bubble count, and why?
vocab: Light intensity drops with the square of the distance: twice as far gives ¼ of the light.
Something that takes in more CO₂ than it releases, like forests and oceans.
